Am I required to buy it?

Only if your home is in a high-risk zone (A or V) and your mortgage is from a federally regulated lender, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Check your zone on FEMA's flood map.

76.7% of Nevada's NFIP policies are in high-risk zones (not 76.7% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

How much does it cost here?

Typically about $857 a year ($71 a month), fees included. Half of homeowners here pay between $695 and $1,060. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $695 · Typical $857 · A quarter pay over $1,060 · A tenth pay $1,299 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 5,827 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price; a brand-new policy is priced at full risk.

Coverage in force: $2.1 billion of building and $433.0 million of contents coverage across all Nevada policies.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy, but there is no wait if you buy it with a new or refinanced mortgage.

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood insurance is bought separately, through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Exceptions: no wait if you buy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, or change coverage at renewal; a one-day wait if a map revision puts the property in a high-risk zone and you buy within 13 months of the revision (44 CFR §61.11). To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. If FEMA aid pays to repair a home in a high-risk zone, you must buy and keep flood insurance on it, or you cannot get that aid again after a later flood. Past aid paid here is in “Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?” below.

Source: floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, fema.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Floods here have led to 1,964 NFIP flood claims and $47.4 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 1997, 2005 and 2017.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 1997 ($19,735,375), 2005 ($10,630,370), 2017 ($3,466,645). Total paid $47,386,497: net building + contents payments by year of loss. Claims are matched by the claims dataset's county code, which may not exactly match a policy's property county.

That is 1,964 claims since 1978 against 9,160 policy units in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Do flood claims here actually pay out?

Most do: 65.4% of claims here paid something. The average paid claim was $36,905.

  • Average paid claim, incl. code-upgrade (ICC) pay$36,905
  • Closed with no payment34.6%
  • Claims that paid1,284

FEMA lists reasons a claim closes without payment, such as damage below the deductible, no flood as the policy defines it, or seepage and drain backup the policy does not cover. The average is over claims that paid something and includes Increased Cost of Compliance payments (help to elevate or rebuild to code), which the yearly totals above leave out. Dollars are as paid at the time, not adjusted for inflation; a single home can file across several floods over the years.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for 36.2% of insured single-family homes here: FEMA's records put their rebuilding cost above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 3,654 policies reporting one)36.2%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)79.9%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 1,175 claims paid with a damage figure)2.6%

Rebuilding cost is the replacement-cost figure on single-family primary-home policies that report one; many owners insure to the building maximum even when that figure is lower, so the two shares measure different things. The damage share counts every paid claim with a damage figure, all building types.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Source: floodsmart.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Why do sites quote different averages for Nevada?

Because they measure different things. From the same FEMA records, the typical single-family home pays $857 a year, but the average across every policy type is $1,218.

MeasureAmountWhat it counts
Median cost, single-family homes$857premium plus fees; the middle policy
Average (mean) cost, single-family homes$933pulled up by a few expensive policies
Median premium only, single-family homes$665before the federal fee, reserve fund and surcharge
Average premium only, single-family homes$730the figure many sites quote
Median cost, every policy type$899adds condos, rentals and businesses
Average cost, every policy type$1,218

Published averages rarely say which of these they are, or which year. All six here come from the NFIP policies in force on July 31, 2026.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

33.8% of policies here pay less than FEMA's full-risk price, so their bills are rising toward it. Median premium $665, full-risk $692 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$665
  • Median full-risk premium$692
  • Pay below full-risk33.8% of 5,827

Yearly cap: Those prices step up toward full-risk each year, limited by the yearly cap. By law a primary home's premium cannot rise more than 18% a year; some policies, such as second homes and businesses, can rise up to 25%. The cap usually does not apply to new policies, and fees and surcharges sit outside it. Bills already at full risk still change with FEMA's yearly rate updates.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $1.7 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $6,555 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Hurricane aid includes wind damage. COVID, fire, ice-storm and tornado aid are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Are these counts complete?

Every record FEMA's download lists was received and counted. FEMA also publishes a separate official policy count, which we have not yet compared for Nevada.

In-force count: 9,160 policy units (from 8,905 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). Download check: policies: 8,905 of 8,905 fetched; claims: 1,964 of 1,964 fetched.

What this data cannot tell you

  • Your own premium — it depends on elevation, coverage and deductible. We show where existing policies fall.
  • Private (non-NFIP) flood insurance prices.
  • Your address's exact flood zone — use FEMA's Flood Map Service Center.
  • Why any one premium changes — we show the gap to full-risk, not the cause.
  • A year-over-year premium trend — the in-force snapshot holds only current-term policies, so a like-for-like multi-year index isn't possible from this data. A per-effective-year median is shown only where several years of policies exist.
